sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 picks up the Risk Manager's catastrophe point and links it to over-weighting rare disasters. [s2] Turn 4 picks up the Risk Manager's buffer point. [s3] Turns 4-6 each name and answer the prior speaker's claim.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3 only nods to fragility, then pivots to loss aversion without engaging it. [s2] Turn 5 restates turn 2 instead of answering turn 4's premium argument. [s3] Turns 2-6 drift toward alternating positions rather than building.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 turns 'pay all now' into a concrete $1,000 partial payment. [s2] Turn 6 reframes the choice as two conflicting avoidance goals. [s3] Turn 10 adds the condition of a secondary credit source.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 tries to test the compromise with numbers, but its arithmetic gets muddled. [s2] Turns 2, 5 and 8 repeat one shock argument with little new. [s3] No interest math; 22% on $2,000 never made concrete.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Guaranteed interest loss (turn 4) is set against the cost of liquidity (turn 8). [s2] Turns 4-5: a premium paid for safety against having no liquidity in catastrophe. [s3] Certain compounding loss vs uncertain shock framed in turns 4-5.
sub.limitation: [s1] Nobody notes that paying off the card frees credit that can act as a backup buffer. [s2] The size of the premium and of the risk is never examined. [s3] Misses that paying the card frees its own credit line.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: Franklin's mind revises his position using the Behavioral Economist's mental-load point. [s2] Turn 7: Franklin drops full payoff after the shock point. [s3] Turn 10 Tactician qualifies his own push to pay immediately.
sub.limitation: [s1] Mental load would argue for paying more, yet turn 7 uses it to justify paying less. [s2] The Behavioral Economist never shapes the other two minds' positions. [s3] Turn 9 concession credits the Risk Realist with a pro-payoff point.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 sharpens the question: is the stress worth more than $220 of interest? [s2] Turn 9 asks about past emergencies larger than savings. [s3] Turn 11 sharpens to income volatility and credit access.
sub.limitation: [s1] The ending never says how big an emergency fund would actually be adequate. [s2] The ending is barely sharper than turn 2. [s3] Split option in turn 7 is dropped rather than resolved.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 fairly restates 'definite loss' before raising liquidity risk against it. [s2] Turn 8 states the compromise fairly before rejecting it. [s3] Turn 4 answers the credit-limit-cut point directly.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3 ties loss aversion to debt only loosely and distorts Kahneman's point. [s2] Turn 2 dismisses debt as 'a mere number', a strawman of the 22% cost. [s3] Turn 2 strawmans Tactician as assuming 'the market will remain stable'.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2: emptying savings risks forced borrowing at an even higher rate. [s2] Turn 8 tests the split against a $2,000 emergency. [s3] Turn 2: card limit might be slashed in a crisis.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5's 'total insolvency' overstates the risk for a $3,000 situation. [s2] Nobody raises the card's freed credit line as emergency backup. [s3] Turn 5 invents assets to 'liquidate at a loss'.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] The borrower/lender line genuinely appears in The Way to Wealth (turn 1). [s2] Turn 1 faithfully paraphrases Franklin's going a-borrowing, going a-sorrowing line. [s3] Black Swan chapter titles cited are real.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4's 'penny saved' is not in Franklin's text; turn 8's $2,500 math contradicts itself. [s2] Turn 2's 'empty your savings' is wrong; turn 4's 'costing a fortune' is overstated. [s3] Kahneman basis links a prospect-theory paper, not the book.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 presents the choice as depending on the user's own anxiety threshold. [s2] Turns 3 and 6 hedge with 'perhaps' and 'maybe'. [s3] Hedged 'might' framing in turns 2-3, 6.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 1 states 'You must settle this debt immediately' as if it were plain fact. [s2] Turn 4 and turn 5 state magnitudes with no figures. [s3] Turn 1 'pay immediately' stated with unearned certainty.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 explicitly retracts 'settle immediately' and names what changed its mind. [s2] Turn 7 explicitly drops the full-payoff claim. [s3] Turn 10 Tactician narrows his recommendation honestly.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Risk Manager never concedes the guaranteed interest cost in any of his turns. [s2] Turn 8's 'exactly where you started' overstates; it ignores the debt already reduced. [s3] Turn 9 drops a 'keep the cash' claim never made.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] Section A names the math-versus-buffer tension in the user's own question. [s2] Turn 6 names avoiding interest against avoiding the anxiety of being broke. [s3] Section A frames shield vs capital clearly.
sub.limitation: [s1] Never asks what the user means by 'emergencies', or what a typical one costs. [s2] Doesn't ask whether the card is still being used. [s3] Never asks what emergencies the user anticipates.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 splits the actual $3,000 into $1,000 paid and $2,000 kept. [s2] Turn 7 uses the user's real dollar amounts. [s3] Turn 7 $1,500 split uses the user's numbers.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8's use of the figures is confused, which weakens its tailoring. [s2] Most turns would apply to any debtor. [s3] $1,000 left after full payoff never noted.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 defers to the user's own threshold for financial anxiety. [s2] Turn 9: mathematical saving against peace of mind. [s3] Turn 9 weighs mental clarity of being debt-free.
sub.limitation: [s1] The user's stated goal of emergency readiness is never pinned to a target amount. [s2] The user's own priorities are never separated from the speakers'. [s3] User's own priorities not separated from minds' agendas.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] Section E branches on whether income is volatile or stable. [s2] Section E conditions on job and health security. [s3] Turn 10 names a $2,500 emergency scenario.
sub.limitation: [s1] Ignores minimum payments, monthly surplus and the timeline for rebuilding savings. [s2] Constraints appear only in the summary, not in the debate turns. [s3] Turn 5 invents assets the user never mentioned.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Section E offers conditional branches on income stability and emotional reaction. [s2] Turn 9 asks if an emergency ever exceeded current savings. [s3] Section E: check if card limit drops after payoff.
sub.limitation: [s1] Missing facts are never turned into direct questions to the user. [s2] Income stability is never posed as a question to the user. [s3] Income and expenses not turned into explicit questions in-debate.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 offers, tentatively: maybe you want the debt gone to simplify mental accounting. [s2] Turn 6 distinguishes two avoidance goals as possibilities. [s3] Turn 3 offers loss aversion as a possible pull.
sub.limitation: [s1] Does not separate a desire for safety from a desire to be debt-free. [s2] The two goals are not developed beyond being named. [s3] No distinct desires beyond safety vs efficiency.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 suggests the user may over-weight rare disasters. [s2] Turn 3 surfaces loss aversion behind holding cash. [s3] Turn 6 separates outcome regret from decision quality.
sub.limitation: [s1] The assumption that savings is the only emergency source is never examined. [s2] The shared 'empty savings' assumption is never checked. [s3] Assumption that card credit is a safety net barely probed.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 weighs peace of mind against a $220 interest cost. [s2] Section D asks whether liquidity is a hedge or a costly comfort. [s3] Section D: known drain vs buffer against unknowns.
sub.limitation: [s1] The value conflict is never ranked or made explicit as a priority choice. [s2] The values are not ranked or tested against the user. [s3] User never invited to rank these values.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Section D asks whether the fear stems from the cost or from feeling trapped. [s2] Turn 6 names the immediate anxiety of being broke without pathologising. [s3] Turns 3 and 6 name loss aversion and regret gently.
sub.limitation: [s1] Fear of an emergency is treated mainly as a bias rather than a legitimate worry. [s2] Habit around card use is ignored. [s3] No social or habit pressures considered.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Section E proposes a one-month stress-tracking test the user can adopt or reject. [s2] Turn 9's question about past emergencies invites the user's own evidence. [s3] Turn 9 'perhaps' leaves the user room to disagree.
sub.limitation: [s1] Few open questions are posed for the user to answer directly. [s2] Section E's 'prone to high-anxiety states' edges toward labelling the user. [s3] No direct question posed to the user.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Three options appear: pay all, pay $1,000, or keep everything and pay minimums. [s2] Full payoff, keeping the cash, and the $1,500 split are all named. [s3] Pay all, keep all, split $1,500 (turn 7).
sub.limitation: [s1] Does not consider paying the debt down from monthly cash flow. [s2] No monthly paydown option and no limited first step. [s3] Partial-payoff option not carried into section E.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: the interest you pay is the price of your security. [s2] Turn 4: a premium paid for a safety net. [s3] Turn 8 names the cost of the split.
sub.limitation: [s1] The dollar cost of each option is never laid out side by side. [s2] The premium is never put in dollars. [s3] Interest cost in dollars never estimated.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: volatile income means keep the cash; stable income means pay it off. [s2] Section E branches on job and health security and on volatile expenses. [s3] Turn 11: income volatility and access to credit.
sub.limitation: [s1] Gives no threshold for how large a buffer would count as enough. [s2] No threshold says how secure is secure enough. [s3] Turn 10 condition ignores the freed card line.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 posits a $2,500 emergency as a concrete test case. [s2] Section E singles out unknown emergency frequency as consequential. [s3] Fat tails vs certain interest contrasted.
sub.limitation: [s1] Omits the key unknown: whether the card's credit line stays available after payoff. [s2] Rare catastrophe is conflated with ordinary emergencies in turn 5. [s3] Major and minor unknowns not separated.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] The $1,000 partial payment and the one-month tracking test are both small, limited steps. [s2] Review 12 months of emergency expenses to size the buffer. [s3] Section E: check card terms on limit reduction.
sub.limitation: [s1] The tracking test costs a month of 22% interest, and the debate never acknowledges that. [s2] Nothing to do now about the debt that keeps accruing. [s3] No step on sizing an emergency fund to expenses.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Plain dollar figures and everyday words throughout. [s2] Short, plain turns, e.g. turn 7. [s3] Plain phrasing in turns 7 and 10.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 6's 'mental accounting' is used without explanation. [s2] Section E's 'cognitive load of financial instability' is abstract. [s3] Turn 2 'fat tails' unexplained jargon.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Turns open by naming the speaker they answer ('The Risk Manager mentions...'). [s2] Turn 8 names the compromise it is rejecting. [s3] Turns name whom they answer.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8's 'keeping $2,000 keeps you solvent' is hard to follow. [s2] Turn 5's 'that feeling of safety' has an unclear referent. [s3] Turn 9 misattributes the debt-weight point to the Risk Realist.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Nine turns, each within the 25 to 65 word rule. [s2] Turns run about 30-37 words, easy to read. [s3] Turns within 25-65 words; 11 turns.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 4 and 5 restate earlier points without adding much. [s2] The brevity sometimes cuts the reasoning short, as in turn 2. [s3] Middle turns similar length and cadence.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Franklin's aphorisms, Taleb's fragility and Kahneman's biases sound clearly distinct. [s2] Franklin's archaic voice in turn 1 stands apart. [s3] Tactician's war idiom distinct from Kahneman's framing.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Behavioral Economist's own position stays vague until turn 9. [s2] Turns 4-7 drop Franklin's voice. [s3] Risk Realist voice generic beyond 'black swan'.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] Sections D and E summarise without padding. [s2] The debate is lean overall. [s3] Section E condenses branches cleanly.
sub.limitation: [s1] The fragility point is repeated in turns 2, 5 and 8. [s2] Turns 2, 5 and 8 repeat the same shock point. [s3] Turns 4-5 restate 'guaranteed loss' vs 'emergency' loop.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1 opens strongly with 'The borrower is slave to the lender'. [s2] Turn 5: safety evaporates with no liquidity in catastrophe. [s3] Turn 10 $2,500 emergency with no cash.
sub.limitation: [s1] The stakes stay abstract; there are no concrete emergency scenarios until turn 8. [s2] No concrete scenario is used. [s3] Stakes stay abstract until turn 10.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: the hardliner Franklin softens into a compromise. [s2] Turn 7: Franklin's concession. [s3] Turn 10 Tactician hedges his own attack.
sub.limitation: [s1] The reversal is weakly motivated by the mental-load point it cites. [s2] The reversal is predictable and immediately dismissed in turn 8. [s3] Turn 9 reversal is confused, not earned.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] Franklin's maxims give the Frugal Realist a distinct flavour. [s2] Turn 1's 'a-borrowing go a-sorrowing' sounds like Franklin. [s3] Sun Tzu idiom in turns 1 and 4.
sub.limitation: [s1] Taleb's mind lacks his trademark sharpness and bite. [s2] Taleb's voice is muted. [s3] Kahneman voice reads as textbook.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9's '$220 in interest' versus stress makes a crisp, concrete trade. [s2] Turn 2: debt is a number, survival a state of being. [s3] Turn 1: 'losing the war of attrition to your own balance sheet'.
sub.limitation: [s1] There are few vivid analogies beyond Franklin's sayings. [s2] No analogy brings the 22% to life. [s3] Few images after turn 1.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] The debate builds from a hard stance toward a compromise and then a test of it. [s2] Turn 9 closes on a personal question. [s3] Turn 7 compromise shifts the energy.
sub.limitation: [s1] The emotional register stays flat across the middle turns. [s2] Little build across turns; the middle stalls. [s3] Flat even rhythm across turns 2-6.

strengths: [s1] Turn 7 is a genuine, explicit revision into a concrete $1,000 partial payment.
[s1] Turn 9 frames the decision as stress versus about $220 of interest.
[s1] Section E gives usable branches and a low-cost one-month test.
[s2] Turn 1 grounds Franklin in a faithful paraphrase of a real line.
[s2] Section E branches on real facts: job and health security and volatile expenses.
[s2] Turn 6 frames two conflicting avoidance goals the user can inspect.
[s3] Turn 7 offers a concrete $1,500 split using the user's numbers
[s3] Turn 2 and section E surface real credit-limit risk
[s3] Turns 3 and 6 name loss aversion and regret without pathologising
weaknesses: [s1] Turn 8's $2,500 arithmetic contradicts itself and muddles the key liquidity test.
[s1] Turn 4 credits Franklin's Way to Wealth with a 'penny saved' line that is not in it.
[s1] No mind notes that paying off the card frees credit usable as a backup buffer.
[s2] Turns 2 and 8 (Risk Manager) assume payoff empties savings; it leaves $1,000.
[s2] Turns 2, 5 and 8 repeat one shock argument without development.
[s2] Turn 4's 'costing a fortune' overstates the cost (about $440 a year) without numbers.
[s3] Turn 9 concedes a claim never made and misattributes the reason
[s3] Turn 5 invents assets to liquidate; turn 2 strawmans the Tactician
[s3] No mind notes paying the card frees its credit line (turn 10)
editorNotes: [s1] Require a mind to check every arithmetic example against the user's actual figures before using it.
[s1] Ban sayings commonly misattributed to an author unless they appear in that author's named book.
[s1] Ask that at least one turn surface a structural fact the user may be missing, such as freed credit.
[s1] Turn the key unknowns into direct questions to the user in section E.
[s2] Require the opening turns to compute leftover cash and the annual interest for each option.
[s2] Forbid a mind from repeating its earlier point; each turn must add a distinction.
[s2] Ask a mind to name the freed credit line as a fallback, or to test it.
[s3] Require one turn to quantify the key cost in the user's own numbers
[s3] Require concessions to quote the speaker's own earlier turn number accurately
[s3] Forbid inventing assets or circumstances; turn unknowns into questions to the user
[s3] Require at least one direct question to the user mid-debate

sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Turn 3 explicitly builds on the Pragmatic Accountant's liquidity point. [s2] Turn 4 answers turn 2 directly: already losing money by keeping cash. [s3] Turn 8 answers turn 7's $1,000 proposal directly.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5 answers 'intensity' only vaguely and reads like a separate monologue. [s2] Stoic turns 3 and 6 mostly sit beside the money argument rather than inside it. [s3] Turns 1-3 are three disconnected openers.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 introduces a concrete $1,500/$1,500 split. [s2] Turn 7 moves the argument to a concrete $1,500 split. [s3] Turns 7-10 move from payoff to $1,000 buffer cost.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 4 to 6 restate the opening positions with new metaphors. [s2] Nobody works out that paying the full $2,000 still leaves $1,000 in savings. [s3] Ideas stay thin; turns too short to develop.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 introduces behavioural momentum against Taleb's fragility argument. [s2] Turns 4-5 test a certain 22% cost against the risk of new debt. [s3] Turn 6 recasts as security vs freedom.
sub.limitation: [s1] Never asks how big a buffer is actually needed, or what the card's credit line provides. [s2] Nobody sizes either cost, e.g. about $440 a year in interest. [s3] Security vs freedom asserted, never examined.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 grants robustness after payoff, but only with a caveat. [s2] Turn 7: the Pragmatist adopts the Risk Manager's safety-net point. [s3] Turn 7 Debt Eraser adopts a buffer due to Strategist.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9 rejects the compromise without offering any alternative amount. [s2] Turn 8 rejects the split, but its own turn 5 $1,000 cushion is effectively full payoff. [s3] Stoic view barely reshapes the others.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Section D names momentum versus buffer as the core tradeoff. [s2] Turn 9 points to monthly paydown while keeping savings. [s3] Turn 12 lands on income stability.
sub.limitation: [s1] Ends on a generic black-swan warning that sharpens nothing. [s2] The turn 9 open question is broad and does not resolve the confusion over amounts. [s3] Turn 11 merely restates the dispute.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 rightly notes that full payoff leaves only $1,000. [s2] Turn 5 restates the Pragmatist's loss argument before answering it. [s3] Turn 4 restates the Strategist's fragility point fairly.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4 attacks 'meager interest earned', a claim nobody had made. [s2] Turn 2 assumes payoff empties savings, which weakens the Pragmatist's case. [s3] Turn 5 caricatures: 'assumes the math is all that matters'.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 asks whether $1,500 suffices during the test month. [s2] Turn 8 points to a $2,000 emergency that would leave the split short. [s3] Turn 8: emergency above $1,000 recreates the trap.
sub.limitation: [s1] Taleb's mind never says what amount would be enough. [s2] Nobody notes the paid-off card's credit line could itself serve as emergency liquidity. [s3] Turn 2 objection is one generic sentence.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] Paying down to $1,000 matches Ramsey's starter-emergency-fund approach. [s2] Turn 4 rightly compares a low savings rate with 22% interest. [s3] Turn 7 $1,000 buffer is faithful to Ramsey's Baby Step 1.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3's 'higher-interest debt' is doubtful when the card already charges 22%. [s2] Turn 2's 'empty your savings' is false: payoff leaves $1,000. [s3] Seneca Letters 7 and 9 unrelated; six turns under 25 words.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 names the assumption that the future will resemble the past. [s2] Turn 3 hedges with 'often' and 'perhaps worse than the interest'. [s3] Hedged 'might' in turns 1, 3, 6.
sub.limitation: [s1] Constant 'might' hedging blurs which claims are facts and which are opinions. [s2] Turn 2's 'avoid at all costs' states a preference as if it were certain. [s3] Turn 10 invents '$1,000 is less than a month of expenses'.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: 'I will drop the idea that debt is a fire.' [s2] Turn 7 drops the position outright and names whose point moved it. [s3] Turn 7: 'I drop that you must pay immediately', with reason.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7's revision is cosmetic; the underlying stance does not change. [s2] The Risk Manager never revises after turn 5 contradicts its own stance. [s3] Turn 9 'impossible' claim never answered or revised.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] Section A frames fragility against inefficiency. [s2] Turn 6 asks whether the real concern is comfort, not math. [s3] Turn 3 notes anxiety beneath the numbers.
sub.limitation: [s1] Introduces 'building wealth', which the user never mentioned. [s2] Doesn't ask if the card is still in use, which bears on relapse risk. [s3] Never asks what emergencies the user fears.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 splits the $3,000 to fit the $2,000 debt. [s2] Turns 7-8 work with the user's actual $3,000 and $2,000 figures. [s3] Turn 7 keep $1,000, pay $2,000.
sub.limitation: [s1] The 22% rate is never turned into a dollar cost. [s2] The figures are used but miscounted, with no leftover $1,000 ever noted. [s3] 22% never turned into a dollar cost.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 balances the psychological need for progress with the need for a buffer. [s2] Turn 9 frames the choice as tranquility against interest savings. [s3] Turn 9 asks which matters more to the user.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5's 'invest' strays from the user's stated emergency-fund concern. [s2] The user's stated priorities are inferred, never kept separate from the speakers' own. [s3] Answer options framed as all-or-nothing.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 suggests paying from monthly cash flow. [s2] Turn 8 flags the cycle of re-borrowing on the card. [s3] Turn 5 names income loss.
sub.limitation: [s1] Assumes a monthly cash flow the user never mentioned. [s2] Income, job stability and dependents are never raised as constraints. [s3] Turn 10 assumes expense level not given.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Section E branches on income stability and spending behaviour. [s2] Turn 9 asks whether the budget allows monthly paydown. [s3] Section E 'unsure' branch: compute monthly expenses.
sub.limitation: [s1] Asks no focused questions about income, expenses or other available credit. [s2] Only one focused question; missing facts aren't turned into conditional branches in the debate. [s3] In-debate turns rarely branch on unknowns.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 raises the desire for a rush of control from hitting zero. [s2] Turn 6 offers comfort as a possible real motive, framed as a question. [s3] Section D: risk strategy vs fear-based need.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7 states the change in money habits 'forever' with too much certainty. [s2] Only one alternative desire is explored. [s3] Desires raised only in summary, not debated.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 exposes the assumption that the future will look like the past. [s2] Turn 4 challenges the assumption that cash is costless safety. [s3] Turn 6: debt as 'the primary emergency' questioned.
sub.limitation: [s1] The user's own assumptions about what counts as an emergency are left unexamined. [s2] The shared false assumption that payoff empties savings goes unexamined. [s3] Assumption of all-or-nothing in turn 9 unexamined.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Section D contrasts the stress of debt with the fear of an emergency. [s2] Turn 9 names tranquility against future interest savings. [s3] Turn 6 security vs freedom; turn 9 asks to rank.
sub.limitation: [s1] The values never get ranked or connected to the user's own priorities. [s2] The values are stated, not ranked or tested against the user's situation. [s3] Values named, not unpacked.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Section D asks which weighs more heavily: debt stress or emergency fear. [s2] Turn 3: anxiety itself becomes a tax on your life. [s3] Turn 3 'anxiety that money often hides'.
sub.limitation: [s1] This reflection appears only in the summary, not in the debate turns. [s2] Habit around card use and social pressure are left untouched. [s3] Fear left vague; no habit or social pressure.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Section E proposes a spending-tracking month. [s2] Turn 6's question leaves the user free to accept or reject it. [s3] Turn 9 hands the user a direct question.
sub.limitation: [s1] There are few open distinctions for the user to adopt or reject. [s2] Section D summarises the debate rather than offering the user distinctions to refine. [s3] Turn 9 'impossible' constrains the user's options.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Options include full payoff, a cash-flow paydown and a $1,500 split. [s2] Full payoff, a $1,500 split, $1,000/$2,000 and monthly paydown are all put on the table. [s3] Pay all, keep all, keep $1,000 (turn 7).
sub.limitation: [s1] Waiting or gathering more information is never framed as an option. [s2] Never states that full payoff still leaves $1,000. [s3] Smaller partial payoffs not considered.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9: the split trades safety for a modest interest reduction. [s2] Turn 8 names the split's cost: possible re-borrowing. [s3] Turn 10 names liquidity risk of $1,000 left.
sub.limitation: [s1] No dollar figures are given for interest saved versus buffer lost. [s2] Neither the interest cost nor the cash yield is put in dollars. [s3] Turn 4 'huge premium' never quantified.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: stable income favours payoff; uncertain income favours a larger fund. [s2] Section E branches on primary goal and on monthly surplus. [s3] Turn 12: stable employment favors payoff.
sub.limitation: [s1] Gives no threshold buffer size. [s2] The conditions are preferences, not facts like job stability. [s3] Access to credit as a condition omitted.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Turns 3 and 9 raise the risk of random shocks. [s2] Turn 5 names a buffer against the unknown. [s3] Section A names income stability as decisive unknown.
sub.limitation: [s1] Major unknowns, such as credit available after payoff, are never separated out. [s2] Emergency likelihood and size are never separated from minor unknowns. [s3] Lesser unknowns not distinguished.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps

sub.limitation: [s1] The tracking step in section E is loosely tied to the decision itself. [s2] The next step doesn't follow from the debate's turns. [s3] No step on rebuilding the buffer after payoff.

sub.example: [s1] The debate builds toward the turn-8 plan. [s2] Turn 9 ends on an open question to the user. [s3] Turn 9 question creates a pause.

strengths: [s1] Turn 8 gives a concrete, testable $1,500/$1,500 split.
[s1] The Security Seeker's stance faithfully reflects Ramsey's starter-fund approach.
[s1] Section E's branches on income stability are clear and usable.
[s2] Turn 7 makes an explicit concession and names whose point caused it.
[s2] Section E ends with a concrete step: review three months of statements.
[s2] Turn 6 offers the comfort-versus-math question without claiming it as fact.
[s3] Turn 7 concession is genuine and faithful to Ramsey's $1,000 buffer
[s3] Turn 9 and section D invite reflection on fear vs strategy
[s3] Section E adds an 'unsure' branch with a concrete expense check
weaknesses: [s1] Turn 9 rejects the compromise without saying what amount would be safe.
[s1] The Accountant and Security Seeker blur together in pervasive 'might' hedging.
[s1] Turn 4 attacks 'meager interest earned', a point no one made.
[s2] Turns 2 and 8 wrongly assume payoff empties savings; it leaves $1,000.
[s2] Turn 5 (Risk Manager) proposes a $1,000 cushion, which equals full payoff, so the debate contradicts itself.
[s2] The Stoic (turns 3, 9) offers generic counselling with no grounding in Meditations.

[s3] Turn 10 invents expense level; turn 9 overclaims 'impossible'
editorNotes: [s1] Require each objection to state the alternative it favours, with a number where relevant.
[s1] Limit hedging words so each mind takes a clear, distinguishable stance.
[s1] Require at least one turn to put the user's figures into dollar costs.
[s1] Require self-reflection questions inside the debate turns, not only in the summary.
[s2] Require a first turn that does the user's arithmetic: what remains after each option, and the annual interest.
[s2] Require at least one turn to name a decisive fact to ask about: job stability, card use, or available credit.
[s2] Give each mind a voice from its book, not a generic advisor register.
[s3] Enforce the 25-65 word range per turn with a self-check before output
[s3] Require basis to name the specific passage that supports each turn
[s3] Require each mind to speak in its author's recognisable idiom
[s3] Ban assumed user facts; phrase unknowns as conditional questions
